newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's KWV set on restructure despite Hanekom.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's KWV set on restructure despite Hanekom.

text.p: South Africa's major wine producer KWV said on Wednesday it was determined to convert itself from a cooperative to a private company despite hurdles set in its way by Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom.

KWV chairman Lourens Jonker told the cooperative's annual general meeting that his board felt the "greatest displeasure" at Hanekom's intervention in the process, which had been due to be completed this month.
Hanekom won a court application which effectively blocks the conversion at least until the new date for legal argument, August 18.
"The ruling entails that KWV's proposed date for the conversion has to be postponed, probably until September 1997," Jonker said.

"I would like to emphasise that no delay will cause KWV to deviate from its goal... the conversion will be to the benefit of consumers in the international markets, as well in the interest of the broader South African wine community and its workers," he said.

KWV, statutory regulator of the domestic wine industry, sells wine and brandy in about 50 countries. It used be the dominant South African exporter until markets opened up with the demise of apartheid sanctions.
Hanekom sought the delay in KWV's conversion partly to allow more time for a study of whether some of the cooperative's assets belonged to the state.
Jonker accused the minister of trying to seize the cooperative's wealth.

"The members' proprietary right to the assets of the cooperative is indisputable and so far no proof to the contrary has been submitted. We are not prepared to negotiate in this regard," he said to loud applause from the several hundred wine-farmers at the meeting.

Referring to another issue raised by Hanekom, that KWV might as a private company pose unfair competition to other players in the domestic market, Jonker said this had been resolved in an agreement with wholesalers grouped in the Cape Wine and Spirits Institute.
"KWV will not enter the domestic alcoholic beverages market without giving five years notice to that effect," he said.
Jonker criticised Hanekom's appointment of Michael Fridjhon as his advisor in the dispute with KWV.

"We cannot negotiate with a person who is in direct competition with the South African wine industry and markets and promotes wine products from other wine countries... This obviously places a question mark behind the minister's intentions to negotiate in good faith," Jonker said.
